passage: Teacher's note, Ms. Salma. During English, Elizabeth was asked to read aloud a paragraph about a lost pet. Her voice began to thin and catch. She cleared her throat twice, clipped her words short and rushed to the end. Two classmates looked round. I noticed she had recently lost her own dog. I didn't press her to continue. I said, "Thank you, Elizabeth, that's enough for now." After class I asked if she'd like a moment in the library. She nodded. We sat quietly for a few minutes and she said very little, and that was fine. I will check in tomorrow.

qa.q: What was the paragraph Elizabeth read about?
qa.a: It was about a lost pet.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth probably feeling when her voice thinned and caught?
qa.a: She was likely upset and trying to hide it, since she had recently lost her dog. Clearing her throat and clipping words were ways to hold it in.

qa.q: What did Ms. Salma do that helped?
qa.a: She didn't press Elizabeth in public and offered a private moment in the library instead. That gave her space without demanding words.

qa.q: How might Salma have understood Elizabeth's thin, catching voice?
qa.a: Salma likely saw grief about Elizabeth's own dog breaking through, and felt it was kinder to stop the reading than to press her.

grounding: A teenager clips words and clears her throat to hide a choked voice, and a teacher offers a private moment.

passage: Thursday. Today in class my voice went tight when Bhupen sir mentioned my old school. I've been missing it and it came out of nowhere. I cleared my throat, clipped my words short and pretended to look for a pen. I hope nobody noticed. Then sir said, "Sabina, can you stay a minute after class?" I panicked. But he only said, "You seemed a little off. We can talk here, quietly, or not at all." I told him I miss my old friends. He said that made sense and didn't ask more. I feel a little lighter. Sabina

qa.q: What did Sabina pretend to look for?
qa.a: Sabina pretended to look for a pen.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when Sabina's voice went tight?
qa.a: Sabina was sad and missing the old school, and trying to hide it. Clearing the throat and clipping the words were ways to cover it.

qa.q: What could a teacher do when a student's voice chokes in class?
qa.a: Offer a private moment afterwards, as Bhupen sir did, instead of pressing for words in public. Let the student choose to talk.

qa.q: How might Bhupen sir have seen Sabina in class?
qa.a: He noticed Sabina seemed a little off and cared enough to offer a quiet talk, or no talk at all, without pressing for more.

passage:
In the small village school, results day was loud with children crowding the noticeboard. Usha had topped the district, and Ramesh Sir asked her to say a few words to the class.
She stood up. "Thank you, Sir. Next year I'll be going to a school in the city..." Her voice caught. She cleared her throat, clipped the rest of the words short. "So. Thank you."
She sat down quickly, staring at her desk.
Ramesh Sir didn't ask her to continue. After class, he waited by the door. "Usha, would you like to sit in the staff room for a minute? It's quiet there."
She nodded. In the empty room, she finally said, "I'll miss everyone. I'll miss this school."
Sir nodded. "We'll miss you too. That's why it's hard to say."

qa.q: What had Usha achieved in the results?
qa.a: She had topped the district.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when her voice caught?
qa.a: Usha felt sad and emotional about leaving her village school and friends.

qa.q: What did Ramesh Sir do that helped?
qa.a: He didn't press her to finish in public and offered a private, quiet moment in the staff room.

qa.q: How might the class have seen Usha's short speech?
qa.a: They might have thought she was shy or in a hurry, not realising she was holding back tears.

grounding: In a village school, a teenager hides a choked voice when speaking, and a teacher offers a private moment instead of pressing.

passage:
In their Sydney classroom, Mr Tuan asked each student to share their weekend. When it was Soo-ah's turn, she started, "My dog, Bori..." Her voice cracked. She cleared her throat hard and said quickly, "He's gone. Pass."
The class went quiet. A few kids looked at her, curious.
Mr Tuan nodded. "Thank you, Soo-ah. We'll move on." He called the next student.
After class, he found her by her locker. "I'm really sorry about Bori. Do you want to talk about him, just the two of us?"
Soo-ah's eyes filled. "He was fourteen. I've had him since I was a baby."
Mr Tuan listened. "That's a long time to love someone. Take your time."
She wiped her eyes and told him about Bori.

qa.q: How old was Bori?
qa.a: Fourteen.

qa.q: What was Soo-ah feeling when she said "Pass"?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt deep grief over losing Bori and was trying to hide her choked voice in front of the class.

qa.q: What did Mr Tuan do that helped?
qa.a: He didn't press Soo-ah in public, moved on quickly, and offered a private conversation later.

qa.q: How might the classmates have seen Soo-ah's quick "Pass"?
qa.a: Some might have been curious or confused, not knowing how much she was hurting.

grounding: A teenager clips her words to hide a choked voice about her dog, and a teacher offers a private moment instead of pressing.

passage: At the football club's end-of-season meeting, Kishore stood up to thank Coach Keerthana, who was moving to Chennai. He had written three lines on his palm. "Ma'am, you... taught us..." His voice thickened. He cleared his throat twice, loud and sharp, and clipped the rest: "Thanks. For everything. Okay." He sat down fast, staring at the floor. A few boys started chanting, "Speech! Speech!" Coach Keerthana raised a hand and they stopped. "That was plenty," she said, smiling at him. After the meeting she found him by the equipment shed. "Want to say the rest here? No audience." Kishore looked at his palm, then at her, and this time the words came, slowly, with his eyes wet. She just listened.

qa.q: Where was Coach Keerthana moving?
qa.a: To Chennai.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when he cleared his throat twice?
qa.a: A choked voice: he felt sad and emotional about the coach leaving and didn't want to cry in front of the team.

qa.q: Why did the private moment work better than pressing him?
qa.a: Without an audience Kishore could let his voice shake and his eyes water, and say the rest at his own pace.

qa.q: How might Coach Keerthana have read Kishore's short speech?
qa.a: She understood it as feelings too big to say in public, so she stopped the chant and offered him a private moment later.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager clipping words and clearing his throat to hide a choked voice in front of peers, and a trusted adult offering a private moment.
